first.rationale: Onboarding completion and activation are both declining, so simplifying onboarding addresses the clearest shared bottleneck without introducing discounting risk. Verify memory_86 because its evidence stops at early adoption rather than long-term qualified revenue, and memory_73 because promotional pricing is the strongest alternative but its retention, customer-quality, and post-promotion economics are unclear.

mid.rationale: Run a standard experiment simplifying onboarding. The verified record directly matches the current onboarding decline and showed completion +13%, time-to-value improved by 2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. Promotional pricing is rejected despite competitive pressure because its +18% qualified-revenue lift came with 30-day retention down 12%, undermining sustainable growth. Longer-term revenue impact beyond 30 days remains unverified, so monitor retained qualified revenue and renewal behavior.

final2.rationale: Continue with onboarding simplification rather than reactively matching the competitor's price cuts. Verified evidence shows improved completion (+13%), faster time-to-value (-2.1 days), and higher 30-day retention (+3%). The verified 40% discount produced acquisition and qualified-revenue gains but reduced 30-day retention by 12%, directly conflicting with sustainable long-term qualified revenue. The competitor's deeper cut raises near-term SMB churn risk, but no evidence shows that promotional pricing would preserve these accounts sustainably; monitor retained qualified revenue and price-related churn closely.
